section: Passive Cooling for Hypoxic Ischemic Encephalopathy

claims.manual_text: Infants greater than or equal to 35 weeks gestation diagnosed with Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE) are treated with whole-body cooling to a core temperature of 33.5 degrees Celsius, as a neuroprotective therapy.
claims.summary: The 2026 AAP clinical report describes therapeutic hypothermia to 33.5 to 34.5 °C for neonates with moderate-to-severe HIE born at ≥36 0/7 weeks, the main whole-body cooling trials targeted 33.5 °C (one, ICE, enrolling from 35 weeks), and an NICHD trial in infants 33 to 35 weeks found no reduction in death or disability [Zanelli2026; Shankaran2005; Azzopardi2009; Jacobs2011; Faix2025].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests the 2026 AAP clinical report applies therapeutic hypothermia to neonates with moderate-to-severe HIE born at ≥36 0/7 weeks, with a target of 33.5 to 34.5 °C [Zanelli2026]. AAP's summary of that report states that for infants born at 35 weeks studies have not shown conclusive benefit or harm and that clinicians in select cases may decide with families to use it [HealthyChildren2026]. An NICHD trial in infants 33 to 35 weeks found no reduction in death or disability with hypothermia, with a 74% Bayesian probability of increased death or disability [Faix2025].

evidence.quote: Therapeutic hypothermia to a temperature of 33.5 to 34.5 °C initiated within 6 hours of birth and continued for 72 hours reduces the risk of death or moderate-to-severe neurodevelopmental impairments in neonates with moderate-to-severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) born at ≥36 0/7 weeks of gestation.

This treatment has not shown benefit for infants with mild hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and is also not recommended for preterm infants born less than 36 weeks' gestation. For those born at 35 weeks, studies have not demonstrated conclusive benefit or harm from this therapy, and clinicians in select cases may decide with families to use therapeutic hypothermia.

claims.manual_text: Do not let patients shiver. Counter-warm extremities as needed by wrapping the extremities with a cloth blanket. Consider the use of morphine for individual babies who continue to shiver or who are uncomfortable/agitated.
claims.summary: An expert review states that neonates rarely shiver and describes morphine as standard of care for comfort during hypothermia, but a Cochrane review found no eligible trials, a cohort study advised cautious empiric opioid use, and no retrieved source addresses counter-warming the extremities [McPherson2021; Backe2022; Natarajan2022].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests human neonates rarely shiver during induced hypothermia because they rely mainly on brown fat thermogenesis, while sedation is described as helping prevent stress and shivering at cooling temperatures [McPherson2021]. Morphine is described as current standard of care in an expert review, but a Cochrane review found no trials to support or refute pharmacological pain and sedation management during hypothermia, and a cohort study suggested cautious empiric opioid use because of associated adverse short-term outcomes [McPherson2021; Backe2022; Natarajan2022].
